item.title: @Thom_Wolf：第二家实验室分享困惑度测量数据，支持OpenAI透明度倡议并公布预训练进展
item.description:
A second lab is sharing perplexity measures

@mustafasuleyman：We fully support OpenAI's transparency initiative. Thanks to @merettm @markchen90 @gdb @sama for leading the way.

We all got into this field to build safe AGI that is genuinely good for humanity. One of the hardest parts of AI safety is coordination, and this is a step in the right direction. Many more steps like this will be needed to deliver safe, contained, and aligned AGI in the next few years.

We're committed to sharing our pre-training progress on a common held-out evaluation set. With OpenAI's permission, we report MAI-2 Base on their evaluation set. Its log-perplexity is 0.819, putting it in the same ballpark as the GPT-5.6 Sol base model. Our model uses the same tokenizer as OpenAI, so the numbers are directly comparable.

In the future, to be able to compare across labs we might need to report bits-per-byte (BPB) rather than perplexity since different labs use different tokenizers. We will also need different evaluation datasets - the fact we have access to OpenAI's evaluation dataset is a special case.

Safety and alignment is now the mission. It's the absolute number one most important focus for our industry. And it begins with small, practical steps like these towards better coordination on pacing.

item.title: @hwchase17：LangChain创始人阐述Agent平台未来架构：运行时、可观测性与治理缺一不可
item.description:
this is a great article and strongly agree on many dimensions. it is a great vision of the agent *runtime* of the future

but the runtime is just one part of an agent platform. theres two glaring omissions imo:

1/ observability/evals
2/ governance

the future described here (of self improving agents) is spot on. but in order to achieve that, theres three main pillars

first is the runtime, which John nails here. what he describes closely mirrors what we've built in langsmith - agent server (to deploy agents), sandboxes, and of course deepagents as the agent harness

the runtime contains the *intended behavior* of the agent. and as anyone who has built agents knows, they dont always do what you intend

thats why they need to learn/evolve on the job. in order to that, you need:

observability/evals: this is the "observed behavior" of the agent. what actually happens, what tools are called, how it performs in certain scenarios. this is ESPECIALLY important as the agent evolves - you need to keep eyes on how its evolving, and it will probably end up writing tests for itself

governance: no matter how much the agent evolves, there are certain things you want to enforce. who it calls tools on behalf of, how it uses those tools, how much it can spend. this is where governance (best enforced through an llm gateway and tool gateway) are crucial

we're building all of these in langsmith - if youre struggling with any parts of these, plz reach out!

@john_ssuh：Agent platform of 2027.

This is the end game. This is the blueprint for the one and only application layer software that will exist. Every other software will effectively become databases for this layer, the everything agentic operating system for the million agent swarm to work on top of.

This is obviously the end game vision for the application layer of ChatGPT and Claude. I have reasons to believe that an independent company will own this product layer. But most ADE, "enterprise agent platform", or vertical saas companies, are focused on the wrong things far too narrowly, not technically competent, and do not have the product / technical vision to see this inevitable future.

The correct agent platform that wins will function like the base of a garden, from which customers will plant their unique "seeds" to grow their own plants and trees, managed and evolved by agents, humans, and signals from the sensors of the business. This presents a clearer picture than "factory of a factory" imo.

item.title: @soumithchintala：Inkling-2-Mini本地运行在单张RTX PRO 6000上在KernelBench-Mega取得10.04倍表现
item.description:
to be honest, I didn't expect Mini would do so well on this kernel generation use-case!

@elliotarledge：Inkling-2-Mini running locally on a single RTX PRO 6000 hit 10.04x on KernelBench-Mega, beating Grok 4.7 (6.34x), GPT-6.1-Sol (4.96x), DeepSeek-V4-Flash (4.32x), and Claude Sonnet 5 (3.92x) on the same GPU, while models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Kimi K3.1-Pro, Qwen3.8-Max, and GLM-5.2 failed to pass on RTX PRO 6000.

highlights from the 2.9-hour trace (686k output tokens):
> wrote a single-launch 188-CTA persistent Triton megakernel (1,119 lines) fusing 3 KDA blocks, 1 MLA block, and 4 MoE blocks with global release/acquire atomic barriers (~0.75 us/sync) and zero inter-op kernel launches
> first working fused kernel hit 3.12x; it profiled Mem Busy at 20%, intentionally ran a broken no-barrier build just to isolate sync overhead, then bisected each phase by skipping it one by one
> used the MLA absorb trick so the [ctx, 8192] BF16 matrix is never materialized, merged softmax + A + o into one phase (-2 global barriers/step), and split MoE gate/up to 1 GEMV per CTA
> climbed 3.12x -> 6.82x -> 8.53x -> 10.04x isolated regrade (0.606 ms/tok, 1,650 tok/s at ctx=8192; 1,941 tok/s at ctx=2048)

audited the final 1,119-line solution end-to-end: clean persistent kernel, fresh state and output every step, 9.98x contended vs 10.04x isolated.

item.title: 【回复】@sh_reya：探讨大语言模型上下文层与文件系统的关系及未来逻辑物理数据独立性的发展
item.description:
回复 @sh_reya
100% we can learn a lot from the history of database development to predict the future of context/semantic layers. query processing has always been I/O or memory bound (except the few years prior to vectorized + compiled engines like monetdb & hyper, and today’s expensive AI functions or string functions). in other words, the way to improve performance is to **transfer less data to the LLM** or **transfer data to the LLM faster**, which is exactly what an index or context layer does.

However, new in the AI era is the need for a **high quality** context layer. Quality was easier in traditional DBs because using an index doesn’t impact correctness. Eg with a B-tree, you get the same rows as a full scan, just faster. A context layer is lossy by design, since the LLM only sees what we put in the context (and maybe progressive disclosure like instructions to read more of the data if it wants). So every decision about what to retrieve or summarize is also a decision about correctness, which we don’t know how to rigorously model. It all comes down to having good, company-specific evals, if I may
原帖

回复 @sh_reya
Relatedly I am bearish on file systems for the context layer. It is a weird blip in time right now that LLMs are best at navigating file systems, probably due to training procedures. But we know that it’s a lot of work to learn and remember how to navigate file systems (see 1973 Turing lecture from Charles Bachman; how bullish they were on the programmer/agent as navigator; all to be replaced by Codd and relational data model). the future of context layers is probably in some logical/physical data independence

item.description:

TrendForce sees NAND bit supply up 25-30% next year. Contract prices are projected to fall 0-5% quarter-on-quarter in both the first and second quarters. Weaker smartphone and PC demand plus lower storage per device add pressure.

Samsung and SK Hynix sell most volume to North American big tech on contract prices. Spot drops do not hit their results the same way.
$SKHY
TrendForce still sees general DRAM contract prices rising 5-10% in the first quarter, 3-8% in the second, and 0-5% in the third and fourth. The turning point sits around mid-2028.

Counterpoint sees growth lasting into the first half of 2027. Supply growth and slower demand later could still force a sharp adjustment if the balance shifts earlier. BNK’s Lee Min-hee estimates 2026 DRAM bit demand up 24% while supplier shipments rise 38%.

That gap could build inventory and trigger a steep price drop from the second or third quarter of next year if end demand weakens. No official cut in server DRAM content has appeared yet.

New cleanrooms and lines from SK Hynix and Samsung open between 2027 and 2029. Actual output lags. Third-quarter global DRAM revenue rose 369% year-on-year while bit shipments rose only about 4%. Earnings lean heavily on price.

SK Hynix has LTAs with 14 customers covering more than 50% of 2027-2028 production. Samsung said its 2027 HBM volume is fully sold at agreed prices.

SoftBank booked a 597.2 billion yen loss after canceling a US data-center power contract. Full memory cancellations still look unlikely while AI competition and tight supply continue.

GTA VI is the ultimate victoy of GPU-driven software rendering, relying on tons of mesh shaders & compute shaders.

At the cost of higher complexity, these pipelines make the GPU manage its own workload. It's the only way to cull millions of instances per frame & to stream virtualized geometry.

Otherwise, it's the CPU slowly dispatching draw calls, figuring out what to draw with bounding box culling. It's crude, slow, imprecise and doesn't scale.

We already saw the birth of GPU software rendering in the past thanks to compute shaders:
- Assassin's Creed Unity had GPU culling

item.title: @binarybits：分析指出人工智能实验室追求递归自我改进时可能面临效率与泛化能力的分化
item.description:
"There are two different improvement loops that have been conflated, and they will come apart. The efficiency improvement loop will accelerate, but a broader improvement loop... will require ever-increasing amounts of compute, talent, data, and real-world feedback."

@random_walker：As AI labs race toward Recursive Self Improvement, there’s a possibility that what they are actually racing toward is Recursive Self Extinction — of their business model. Here’s my reasoning.

1. Progress on verifiable tasks continues. In particular, improving the cost efficiency of existing capabilities is a highly verifiable task. For the past few years, cost per equivalent capability has dropped by at least 10x per year. I think this progress will be sustained for a few more years, and even accelerate as labs use AI more and more heavily for AI research in the pursuit of RSI. There is of course a ceiling to efficiency improvements, but I don’t think we’re close to that ceiling.

2. Progress on most unverifiable tasks remains frustratingly hard. AI inherits the same limitations (ambiguous success criteria, slow and noisy feedback) that limit human performance at tasks ranging from writing to governance. The optimization paradigm generally doesn’t result in superhuman capabilities on such tasks, because whatever proxy you optimize for gets Goodharted. item.title: @Whats_AI：构建大模型评判系统：应专注提示词迭代而非过度复杂化架构
item.description:
I've had tons of discussions around LLM judges since working on a benchmark myself.

Turns out, a lot of people overcomplicate LLM judges before they even have a solid prompt.

A collaborator and I were planning our workshop session on ToneBench, and we made a deliberate choice: keep it skills-focused rather than deep AI engineering.

When people build automated evaluation systems, the temptation is to jump straight into complex multi-agent architectures and scoring math.

In reality, getting reliable evaluations comes down to a tight prompt iteration loop.

You write clear evaluation criteria, run the judge against real drafts, find where it misinterprets tone or nuance, and refine the instructions.

Each iteration teaches you more about your edge cases than an elaborate pipeline ever could.

If your LLM judge is giving erratic scores, do not add more infrastructure.

Fix the criteria and tighten the feedback loop first.

The most important part that needs your time is the human calibration. Build this set as soon as you can and use it to iterate with your LLM judges.
